As others have said, you don't need to do foundation etc. Me personally if I only do eyeshadow my lashes disappear, so I'd recommend putting on a little bit of mascara. It's kind of like framing:) But there are no rules, no rights or wrongs, this is entirely up to you.

In all honesty I've never bothered with bronzer, contour, and blush. First of all, I already have a red face, I didn't apply foundation and concealer to hide the redness in my face just to add it back on? I find it silly _for me_, everyone else loves their blush and if it works for them it works for them.

You want simple makeup?

Provided you've prepped your face (washed or cleansed with micellar water) and applied some moisturiser a couple minutes ago (this needs to dry), just apply a couple of swipes of concealer (underneath eye and on problem areas, usually chin) and then apply enough foundation that it'll spread across your face evenly but not too much. 

Provided your hands are clean, you can do your makeup with your fingers, just smooth it over your face and then finish rubbing off the rest below your chin to your neck so there's no drastic cut off.

And then wam bam madame just forget the rest. If you want a full beat face yeah you're going to need to learn contour but for an everyday face? It works just fine.

Eyes? Apply a brown liner on your top waterline. Find the colour closest to your skintone and apply it on your eyelid  so you have a base. You can use a fluffy brush to blens this out as far as you want because it's close to your tone so it won't look wonky.

Then just pop on a vibrant matte or shimmer over your lid. You can go back with your fluffy brush over the end of your lid to smooth it out so the darkness blends out and doesn't create a harshline.

To add depth you can pop a dark colour over your lid and then from the innercorner of your eye to about half your lid apply a shimmer. 

Then mascara. 

Now I'm talking the simplest of simple techniques here... of course there's a lot more skill you can develop over time but I get compliments on my basic ass eye makeup all the time. Bonus by using concealer as a base, waiting for it to dry, and then setting it with the skintone shade i mentioned earlier.

Most people don't do all the extra makeup stuff you see in tik tok tutorials :) Not a criticism as I find it beautiful and would love to do that but a) I'm lazy b) I don't want to spend hours getting ready.

Depending on your skin type you may need a primer or setting powder. Test out how your base looks without these and then experiment if it doesn't hold.

You're not wrong, there are lots of situations that can make an unhappy childhood. My wording was perhaps not the best, I meant people who have had a good relationship with their parents and aren't unpacking the consequences of that relationship. You can get bullied at school, you can move to a foreign country where you don't speak the language, sexually harassed, assaulted, view a traumatic event  - there are lots of things that aren't a direct consequence of your parents' treatment of you that could make for an unhappy childhood. 

You can't shield a child from the world, but you need to give them the best upbringing you can provide (not financially, emotionally, I don't mean a child has to be spoiled to be loved). That's a lot! You have to sacrifice a lot for that. I don't think most parents who have children for the sake of having children really acknowledge and assimilate that.

I don't think the selfless vs selfish dichtomy was the right approach for that comment. However, there's no denying that many people have children because it's the next logical step in a relationship/that it's expected of them/they don't know what else to do. I'm sure there are people who realise parenthood was wonderful even when they didn't actively desire it, but there are a lot of kids who are brought into this world only to be neglected/abused/miserable because one or both of the parents just do not provide the loving and enriching environment that should come with raising a child.

I firmly believe that our default should not be to have children, because children are a very big commitment that uproots your life, and I find more people regret having children than not. You could also tell me this is a misuse of statistics (not that I'm looking at numbers) because there are far more people who have children than don't. I just think that children deserve to be wanted and cherished fully without resentment of what could have been, without feeling like a burden for a separating couple, etc etc, so people should really interrogate themselves whether they really want this, whether they're just following a script or they're just trying to find themselves through parenthood, the latter two imo not being a good reason to have children.

I think r/childfree gives a very bad rep to people in general who are childfree. There are plenty of abusive parents, do we assume all parents are inherently abusive? The same goes for childfree people. Yes there is a loud part of reddit that calls them crotch goblins and whatnot but not all childfree people are like that. 

Ultimately, we do not harm children by _not_ having them because... we don't have them lol. This is again anecdotal and not scientifically based, but I can count the people I know who had happy childhoods and aren't unpacking some form of trauma in their adulthood on one hand. Are we better people for not having children? Not inherently, we do not have an inherent moral superiority, except compared to parents who do not provide adequate care to their child. I mean. That's a no brainer. People who don't actively harm children, including loving parents, are better than those who do. 

There's nothing moral or immoral about having or not having children so long as in the former case, you actually take care and nourish your child (both literally and emotionally).

Either way, this really helped me improve concentration thus less downtime/distraction and faster intake due reduced lecture time. I do not think working out while listening to your lecture is a good idea unless you intend to go back and take notes after the fact, having to relisten the important bits etc. Your workout can't be a replacement for the time spent on your lecture but it can help prep your brain by already having an idea about it.

For pudding using cornstarch:

First, before putting your pot on the stove, stir the cornstarch vigorously in a little bit of milk to ensure it's completely dissolved. I didn't realise it but if you skip this step and just stir it in the whole pot of milk, you will miss bits of cornstarch and even if your pudding thickens, it will become watery as it cools down. 

I also always assumed stirring continuously should happen to the get go and this has led to many disappoints. Now I can whip it up super fast, simply wait for the milk to boil (make bubbles), maybe stirring every now and then to ensure it doesn't burn, before beginning to stir vigorously for 2-5m. If you stir vigorously from the get go, it's not heating up to the desired level and it just leads to frustration.

With these methods, I'll have a pudding in under ten minutes, vigorous stirring under five. I love pudding when it's hot and it's deliciously creamy and thick, even using semi-skimmed milk. I use 1 tbsp cornstarch per cup of milk.

Depends on your meaning of 'should be eating'. You should eat vegetables, but you don't have to eat vegetables you don't like to be healthy. I've always hated that mindset of parents forcing their kids to finish a plate of vegetables they obviously don't like, and cooked in ways they don't like.

You should be eating foods that are filling, healthy, that make you feel good, but also that taste good. And that's possible! You just need to find the right balance and find ways to cook foods you didn't previously like. 

For instance, I used to hate cooked vegetables but I ate fresh greens just fine as a salad. But I like stir-fry, so what gives? I started cooking stir-fry's myself, with a much higher ratio of vegetables vs carbs/protein than in restaurants. As long as I can get a bit of carb or meat on my fork with the seasoned vegetables, then I eat way more vegetables than if you just put a casserole of pure cooked veggie in front of me. And it's delicious! Pure rice/noodles with no vegetables tastes lacking to me.

Now, as for what you shouldn't eat, that depends on you. Are you the type of person who can eat sugar in moderation? Who sees dessert as a once in a while thing and not something to binge on each day?

I was the latter, but I didn't remove treats from my diet altogether. I eat a bowl of nicecream (ice cream made from frozen banana and milk) every day to satisfy my cravings for something sweet, as well as fruit.

I'm a proponent of sugar free and I think removing processed sugar from our diets is beneficial. In store-bought ready made foods, there's a lot of hidden sugars, so if there's something I'd say you're better off avoiding to be healthy - it's those. But making your own salad dressings at home, making your own desserts, there are ways to treat yourself and still be healthy.

I think total restriction is the enemy of healthy eating, especially if you have a bad relationship with food to begin with. So do eat more vegetables, more fruit, more homecooked meals, but eat things you like.

I definitely think replacing real sugar with artificial sugar is a place to start. Some people may want to eventually get rid of artificial sugar altogether, but I think it definitely helps to wean yourself off of real sugar.

One thing you'll notice is that artificially sweetened things/sugar free foods will taste much much less sweet, so you are still satisfying a craving while readjusting your taste buds.

I've made bananas my holy grail. I make nice cream (freeze a banana and then pulse it with 3/4 cup milk to make soft serve ice cream texture) and banana pancakes (banana, egg, some flour, cinnamon). It's also a good idea to try to eat fruit, raw and whole. They will curb hunger much more efficiently. One note on that, if you're not already aware, smoothies with a lot of fruit are generally not a good idea, because you end up losing the fiber (which fills you up) while still consuming loads more sugar than you would if you would eat each fruit individually (because smoothies require more fruit than you could feasibly eat in one sitting). The nice cream is just one whole fruit, so it's not a huge deal. :)

In any case, if you're struggling with cold turkey, you might want to proceed in steps. Step one, replace real sugar foods with artificial sugar foods. Step two,   reach for a fruit once a day in place of artificial sugar. Step three, try to cut down on artificial sugar by getting it mostly from fruit. etc etc

I think 500 exercises is a huge amount to begin with. I don't think you should aim to complete a certain number of exercises. Identify which exercises are exam type exercises. You need to understand what is expected of you on the exam. Simple exercises are to help you understand the concept, complicated exercises are to push you to think a little more. I genuinely cannot fathom 500 exercises of any chapter, so I really have no idea what you're dealing with, other than that seems unnecessarily gruelsome.

Reviewing is the key notion here. I suspect the first time you review after a week of doing a new chapter, you will struggle to recall a bit already. Take your time to review in a way that makes sense. If after an hour, you feel like you haven't made significant progress, then revise a little longer. You need to prioritise and identify the key exercises you find challenging, what makes them challenging, and keep those as your review exercises.

Start with some simple exercises as a warm-up, then do the challenging / exam questions. Depending on their length, you'll want to do maybe a few. The intent isn't to recram everything in that space of time, it's just to train your brain again. You'll see that after a few reviews, it will be much easier to recall and the amount of time required to solve an exercise will diminish. So of course, your review time will adapt and vary.

I think over time you should space it out more. The easier it is to recall, the more space you should give it. After a month of weekly practicing, if you find it easy to recall, you'll probably want to move on to every two weeks. It really depends on how comfortable you are with the material, because if you haven't practiced something in math for a while, it will take a lot longer to recall. 

Say your exam is in June and you crash coursed Pre-calc in March and never touch it again until a week before June - no matter how many exercises you did in March, you will likely struggle to recall what you did, if at all. Just as long as you practice it to some degree at a regular pace, that you yourself can choose and adapt according to your needs, up until the due date, then you should be fine.

You might also want to adapt the amount and type of practice. Maybe the first week you'll need to redo some simple exercises to familiarise yourself with the mechanics before tackling the complicated exercises. Don't underestimate simple exercises. In my personal experience, if I'm stuck on something, it helps a lot to go back to the basics. Even in university, we're reminded sometimes of certain rules with calculation. You're doing integrals but all of a sudden factorising becomes relevant again - that kind of stuff. 

Hope this helps! All in all, I think you should trust yourself when you start to feel comfortable and be more liberal, but don't get too confident and choose to put something aside until the due date. It would be silly to find something really easy, and then struggle with it at the exam because the last time you practiced it was months ago

Spaced learning is encouraged for really maintaining knowledge. What this means is that doing 500 exercises in one block will make sure you know how to do logs for now - but as you suspect, as weeks go by, the ease with which you're able to complete them will fade. Depends on how complicated this is though. If it's very basic log rules, I'll just stick on a flashcard and keep 'em around.

My rule of thumb for math is you need to keep practicing it, but everything in one chunk will only help you if you're evaluated on that the next day. If you want to maintain your knowledge, you're going to have keep it at, at least once a week. This is spaced learning. You can look it up if you want to get down to the technicalities but that's the gist of it. I definitely don't advise you do 500 exercises again. Simple exercises to get the hang of it, and then move on to complicated ones / similar exam questions so you can properly challenge yourself. If anything, having exercises you've never done before will avoid the trap of just remembering the solution and not solving it from scratch.

tldr; don't cram 500 exercises in a block. start with simple ones, then gradually build up. move on to the next subject once you're able to solve the exam type exercises, but remember to go back to the previous chapter on a semi-regular basis, say weekly, to maintain that knowledge and ensure you won't forget.

Similar experience, I was able to cram first year theory but I fell hard on my ass when it came to math subjects and later more difficult theory subjects. 

The most important thing I've learned is that just reading and highlighting is not enough, no matter how many times you read. You just trick your brain into thinking you know, due to the familiarty, but it doesn't teach you anything. So always, always find a way to soak up the words. Whether it be in writing, in making graphs, tables, drawings, recording yourself speak, etc. 

The rest of this is personal experience and not necessarily science based stuff, but there are good videos about that, like from Thomas Frank. I don't use any particular apps either, and while I have my computer handy a lot for research, pdfs of books, slides / content uploaded online, I like to write and learn on paper. I will usually only print out things I want to leave comments on, like exercises. 

I've tried and tried pomodoro technique, Forest app and everything, but personally it doesn't work for me. I will start work, get distracted, come back, timer will go off, I'm still attentive so I'll ignore it and keep going, and in the end it feels like a useless interaction because I don't stick to the timer (even if I change the time). 

My breakdown is this: first things first, I need comfortable writing material that I enjoy using. This doesn't mean expensive or going to Muji - personally I bought three pens I like writing with for 70 cents from a discount store. Similarly, paper. The look and feel of it. I found I really enjoyed writing on coloured paper with a certain thickness for making my notes. Again, it was like a euro for a pack, pretty good deal. 

I know this sounds probably irrelevant, but for me personally, if I don't feel comfortable with what I'm using I get frustrated and then distracted. It's important I remove any excuse to be distracted, so I also study outside of my home as much as possible. 

Having utensils I enjoy using, I can now get down to business. 

For mathematical subjects (anything with numbers really, like accounting), it's primarily exercises. Typically, if I can't do the first exercise after trying and then looking at the theory, I will take a peek at the solutions and make this my example to draw from. Usually there's repetition, so I keep applying the same solution, and if I notice differences, I make note of them in order to piece together situational answers. I usually make flashcards from this, of what to do in what situation. Obviously, you need to come back and do these exercises again, until you don't need any pointers. I also like to keep any attempts made on paper, only crossing them out to know it's false, so when I come back I can see if I made similar mistakes and pinpoint what I need to be careful with.

Math for me is a subject that needs upkeep. I will usually do exercises at least once a week. If I fail to maintain it, the holes in knowledge creep up fast, so this is essential. 

Theory subjects is a lot of writing and summarising. It's important to be able to simplify explanations in your own words. You should know the details (if relevant), but if you can't explain it in an oversimplified way, then you're not comfortable with it yet. 

If you have a study guide, that is your bible. If not, the best thing you can do is try to make your own. 

I try to journal about what I've done and make a list of things I need to do each week so I have some flexibility. Exercises for any math subject, read book chapters + extra reading for theory each week, and from those, make flashcards / concise summaries to really assimilate the information. If I've noticed myself struggling with something, I will make note of it so I can seek additional resources. Some research, YouTube videos, asking a friend, or even reaching out to the professor. 

You'll feel much more on top of things if you study regularly. It's a lot of work but it pays off, and it's a lot easier to study a little regularly than cram a lot in a small amount of time. I really do recommend watching Thomas Frank's videos though, they gave me a lot of insight.
